# Thromboangiitis obliterans

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Vascular diseases > Thromboangiitis obliterans*

[Original Article Link](/library/2h0TWf)

---

## Summary

Thromboangiitis obliterans (<u>TAO</u>), also known as Buerger disease, is an inflammatory, nonatherosclerotic, vasoocclusive disease affecting small and medium-sized vessels of the extremities. <u>TAO</u> most commonly affects adult male individuals with a significant history of tobacco consumption (e.g., smoking, chewing, vaping). In susceptible individuals, tobacco exposure causes inflammation of the <u>tunica intima</u>, with the formation of a highly cellular <u>thrombus</u> that occludes the affected vessel. Patients frequently present with <u>intermittent claudication</u>, <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>, and <u>migratory superficial thrombophlebitis</u>. Eventually, <u>chronic limb-threatening ischemia</u> develops and the patient presents with <u>rest pain</u>, absent <u>pulse</u> in the extremities, and/or digital <u>ulcerations</u>. <u>Angiography</u> can determine the extent of the disease and differentiate <u>TAO</u> from other causes of peripheral vasculopathy. The most important therapeutic measure is the complete avoidance of tobacco exposure. Additionally, <u>prostaglandin</u> analogues (e.g., <u>iloprost</u>) may be used to improve <u>ulcer</u> healing and decrease <u>rest pain</u>. Patients with <u>TAO</u> who develop <u>gangrene</u> require <u>amputation</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: up to 20 cases per 100,000 individuals  [[1]](/library/x0XER9)

* Sex: : <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (3:1)

* Age of onset: before the age of 45 years [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* The exact etiology of <u>TAO</u> is unknown.

* Tobacco consumption is the single most important <u>risk factor</u> for <u>TAO</u>. [[3]](/library/V1WGf40)

---

## Pathophysiology

<u>TAO</u> is an inflammatory, nonatherosclerotic, vasoocclusive disease affecting small and medium-sized vessels of the extremities.




### Histopathological phases [[4]](/library/p30Ljf)




* Acute phase

* Inflammation of the <u>tunica intima</u> (i.e., <u>endarteritis</u>) with neutrophilic infiltration and microabscess formation

* Inflammation may extend to the <u>tunica media</u> but the <u>internal elastic lamina</u> usually remains intact.

* Formation of a highly cellular inflammatory <u>thrombus</u>

* Intermediate (subacute) phase

* <u>Mononuclear cells</u>, <u>fibroblasts</u>, and <u>giant cells</u> replace <u>neutrophils</u>

* <u>Thrombus</u> organization

* Chronic phase

* Organized <u>thrombus</u>

* The inflammatory process may extend to the adjacent <u>vein</u> and nerve; , resulting in the encasement of the <u>artery</u>, <u>vein</u>, and nerve in a fibrous sheath.

---

## Clinical features

<u>TAO</u> affects the small and medium vessels of the extremities. Other systems are only very rarely involved.




### Extremities [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[5]](/library/P1WWS40)




* <u>Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis</u> (recurrent): often seen prior to the onset of limb <u>ischemia</u> ;  [[3]](/library/V1WGf40)[[6]](/library/ocW0W40)

* Tender <u>nodules</u> along the course of the affected <u>vein</u>

* Induration

* <u>Erythema</u>

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* Chronic or <u>acute limb ischemia</u>: may progress from <u>distal</u> to <u>proximal</u> vessels 

* <u>Intermittent claudication</u>

* <u>Pain</u> at rest, cool extremities, and/or diminished or absent pulses

* <u>Ulceration</u> and/or <u>gangrene</u> of fingertips and/or toes (digits may autoamputate)





> [!TIP]
> <u>TAO</u> typically affects more than one limb. [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[6]](/library/ocW0W40)




> [!TIP]
> Upper extremity <u>ischemia</u> is often asymptomatic; perform an <u>Allen test</u> in all patients with <u>TAO</u>. [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[6]](/library/ocW0W40)




![Toe gangrene](media/k6roagnyzbfplktxqxm9uk59.jpg)

Toe gangrene




### Systemic symptoms [[1]](/library/x0XER9)[[6]](/library/ocW0W40)




* <u>Joints</u>: nonerosive <u>arthritis</u> of <u>large joints</u>

* Organ <u>ischemia</u> (very rare) : e.g., manifesting as <u>colon stricture</u> or perforation in the <u>GI tract</u>, <u>stroke</u> in <u>CNS</u> involvement [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[6]](/library/ocW0W40)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles




* <u>TAO</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> that requires:

* Typical clinical features in a patient with a history of tobacco consumption

* Exclusion of <u>differential diagnoses of TAO</u>

* Imaging studies (i.e., <u>angiography</u> and <u>echocardiography</u>) can be obtained to rule out other embolic sources and support the diagnosis.

* A <u>biopsy</u> may be indicated in patients with atypical presentations.

* Consultation with vascular <u>surgery</u> and/or rheumatology is often required.





> [!TIP]
> Suspect <u>TAO</u> in a patient < 45–50 years old with signs of <u>distal</u> limb <u>ischemia</u> and a history of tobacco consumption.




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[3]](/library/V1WGf40)




The following studies are normal in patients with <u>TAO</u> and should be obtained in all patients to rule out alternative diagnoses:




* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>Liver studies</u>

* <u>BMP</u>

* <u>ESR</u> and <u>CRP</u>

* <u>Autoantibodies</u> (e.g., <u>ANA</u>, RF, <u>anticentromere antibodies</u>)

* <u>Coagulation studies</u> (see “<u>Hypercoagulable states</u>”)





> [!TIP]
> <u>ESR</u> and <u>CRP</u> remain within normal limits, which helps differentiate <u>TAO</u> from <u>vasculitides</u>.




### Imaging studies [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[3]](/library/V1WGf40)




* <u>Angiography</u>  

* Indications

* Patients with a suspected <u>proximal</u> source of <u>emboli</u>

* Patients with confirmed <u>TAO</u> to assess the extent of disease

* Findings

* Segmental occlusions in the <u>distal</u> vessels of the extremities

* Corkscrew-shaped collateral vessels around the site of occlusion

* Normal <u>proximal</u> <u>arteries</u> without evidence of <u>atherosclerosis</u>

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: indicated in patients with a suspected cardiac source of <u>emboli</u>





> [!TIP]
> An <u>angiography</u> is preferred over <u>CTA</u> and <u>MRA</u> because of its higher <u>sensitivity</u> for detecting small vessel disease in the extremities. [[3]](/library/V1WGf40)




### Additional studies




* <u>Ankle-brachial</u> index (<u>ABI</u>): may be decreased  [[3]](/library/V1WGf40)

* Additional <u>laboratory studies</u>: Consider based on the patient's clinical features (e.g., <u>urine drug screen</u>, serum <u>cryoglobulins</u>). [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[3]](/library/V1WGf40)

* <u>Biopsy</u>

* May be considered in patients with tender <u>nodules</u> and/or <u>superficial thrombophlebitis</u>, atypical locations (e.g., large vessel involvement), or age of onset > 45 years [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[5]](/library/P1WWS40)

* Typically shows <u>acute inflammation</u> of all layers of the vessel wall accompanied by occlusive <u>thrombosis</u> [[6]](/library/ocW0W40)

---

## Differential diagnoses

The following alternate diagnoses are typically investigated in a patient with suspected <u>TAO</u>.  [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[3]](/library/V1WGf40)[[5]](/library/P1WWS40)




* <u>Peripheral artery disease</u>; see “<u>Differential diagnosis of claudication</u>.”

* <u>Hypercoagulable states</u>

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u>

* Autoimmune diseases

* <u>Vasculitides</u> (e.g., <u>Takayasu arteritis</u>, <u>Behcet syndrome</u>)

* <u>Localized scleroderma</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### General principles




* There is no specific treatment for <u>TAO</u>.

* Tobacco abstinence is the most important therapeutic measure.

* Pharmacotherapy may improve <u>ulcer</u> healing.

* <u>Revascularization</u> procedures are rarely performed.

* Consult a vascular <u>surgeon</u> and/or a rheumatologist for all patients.





### Prevention and <u>supportive care</u> [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[3]](/library/V1WGf40)




* Abstinence from tobacco in any form (e.g., smoking or chewing tobacco, <u>nicotine</u> patches or <u>gum</u>) 

* Most effective measure for reducing symptoms

* Decreases the risk of <u>amputation</u> if started early in the disease course

* Protection of fingers and toes from cold and mechanical injuries (e.g., wearing gloves and appropriate footwear)

* Basic wound and <u>skin</u> hygiene (e.g., cleaning with soap and water, covering wounds with clean bandages) contributes to <u>ulcer</u> healing and prevents infections. [[1]](/library/x0XER9)





> [!TIP]
> Complete cessation of tobacco consumption in any form is the single most effective therapeutic measure. [[1]](/library/x0XER9)[[3]](/library/V1WGf40)




> [!WARNING]
> Even <u>nicotine</u> patches can reactivate <u>TAO</u>. <u>Bupropion</u> and <u>varenicline</u> are the preferred agents for assisting in <u>tobacco cessation</u>. [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[3]](/library/V1WGf40)




### Symptomatic therapy  [[2]](/library/C0XqR9)[[6]](/library/ocW0W40)




* <u>Calcium channel blockers</u> (<u>nifedipine</u>, <u>amlodipine</u>): commonly prescribed, but evidence of <u>effectiveness</u> is lacking [[1]](/library/x0XER9)

* <u>Iloprost</u> improves resolution of trophic changes and may reduce the <u>amputation</u> rate.





### Surgical therapy [[4]](/library/p30Ljf)[[6]](/library/ocW0W40)




* Patients with <u>ulcers</u> may require <u>debridement</u> and <u>antibiotic therapy</u> for <u>soft tissue infections</u>. [[1]](/library/x0XER9)

* Patients who develop <u>gangrene</u> require <u>amputation</u>.

* <u>Revascularization</u> procedures (e.g., bypass grafting, <u>angioplasty</u>) are rarely feasible because vascular involvement tends to be diffuse and <u>distal</u>.
